sources.note: Section 1.1 Phonology says nothing about accent placement; the only mention is p. 795: 'a reduction of final unaccented /o/ to a sort of schwa ə (?), rendered by epsilon (Πιλαyε, Aπολοδορε)' (citing Brixhe 2018, 1853). No rule for where stress falls.

sources.citation: Duridanov, Ivan. 1985. Die Sprache der Thraker (Bulgarische Sammlung 5). Neuried: Hieronymus.
sources.note: Ch. VII 'Vergleichende Phonetik' (pp. 104-121) has no Akzent section; p. 108 states that unstressed vowels (unbetonte Vokale) were reduced and syncopated in late Thracian (Mygdon, Atlas < *Atulas, Zbel-thurdos); p. 110 speaks of au > o 'vor einer betonten Silbe (*Pautéla, *Potéla)'. A stress accent is presupposed but its position is never stated.

sources.citation: Georgiev, Vladimir I. 1981. Introduction to the History of the Indo-European Languages. Sofia: Bulgarian Academy of Sciences.
sources.note: Section 4.2.2 'Characteristic Features of the Thracian Language' (pp. 117-118) lists sound changes only; the one accent remark is 'On the disappearance of the unstressed vowel cf. Thrac.. > Patrus..' and 'syncope of the unstressed vowel' in Atlas < *adula (ch. 11). 'Under stress' conditions appear only in the Dacian tables (Table 7), not for Thracian. No position rule.

sources.citation: Duridanov, Ivan. The Language of the Thracians (abridged English translation of Duridanov 1976 by V. Karloukovski; ch. 7 = full translation of Duridanov 1985 ch. VII by J. Tchorbadzhijski). kroraina.com
sources.note: Same content in English: 'the unstressed vowels were apparently subject to a reduction, as a result of which they could sometimes even fully disappear'; 'monophthongization of au to o previous to a stressed syllable (*Pautéla, *Potéla)'. No position rule.

tone.quote: Je soulignerai seulement a. que la mutation de la voyelle semble bien encore correspondre à un phénomène aréal, étalé sur de longs siècles ; b. que mutation de / o/, élimination de la consonne finale et sans doute réduction de la géminée à une simple pourraient bien refléter l’émergence précoce, dans la région, d’un accent à dominante intensive [n. 30: Autre manifestation de cet accent: la syncope, cf. dans une dédicace Plae en face du Pilae du n° 5], qui affaiblissait la partie ultime, atone, du mot ; c. que la délabialisation du / o/, sans nécessairement antériorisation, aboutissait sans doute à une voyelle réduite de type schwa, dont E ne donne qu’une image approximative
tone.locator: p. 134, section 4.4 (with n. 28 and n. 30); cf. p. 133 on closing of atonic mid vowels, p. 138 n. 37
tone.translation: I will only stress (a) that the vowel change still seems to correspond to an areal phenomenon spread over long centuries; (b) that the change of /o/, the elimination of the final consonant and probably the reduction of the geminate to a single consonant could well reflect the early emergence, in the region, of a predominantly intensive (stress) accent [n. 30: another manifestation of this accent: syncope, cf. Plae in one dedication beside Pilae of no. 5], which weakened the final, unaccented part of the word; (c) that the delabialisation of /o/, without necessarily fronting, probably resulted in a reduced schwa-type vowel, of which E gives only an approximate picture.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No tone described; the author infers an early, predominantly intensive (dynamic stress) word accent in the Thracian of Zone/Samothrace from weakening of final unaccented syllables (o > schwa written E, loss of final consonants, syncope), i.e. by implication not a pitch accent; accent position not stated.
